title: Ampere's Circuital Law
short_intro: Ampere's circuital law relates the line integral of a magnetic field around a closed loop to the total electric current passing through the surface bounded by the loop. It serves as a fundamental principle in magnetostatics, analogous to Gauss's law in electrostatics.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Direct application of Ampere's law to find magnetic fields due to symmetric current distributions such as long straight wires, infinite sheets, and long solenoids.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Advanced calculations involving toroids, non-uniform current densities, magnetization vectors, verification of Stokes' theorem, and the inclusion of Maxwell's displacement current term.

prerequisites: Biot-Savart law and magnetic field due to steady currents
Line integrals and closed-loop integration in vector calculus
Right-hand thumb rule for the direction of magnetic fields

concept_notes.heading: Statement and Mathematical Formulation
bullets: Ampere's circuital law states that the line integral of the magnetic field B over a closed path is equal to μ<sub>0</sub> times the net steady current I<sub>enclosed</sub> threading through the surface bounded by the path.
Mathematically expressed as ∮ B · dl = μ<sub>0</sub> I<sub>enclosed</sub> in vacuum or free space.
The law is universally valid in magnetostatics, but fails for time-varying electric fields unless Maxwell's displacement current is added.

concept_notes.heading: Choice of Amperian Loop
bullets: An Amperian loop is a hypothetical closed curve chosen for evaluating the line integral of the magnetic field.
To simplify the calculation of B · dl, the loop must possess high symmetry such that the magnitude of B is uniform along the path and B is either parallel or perpendicular to the path element dl.
The shape of the Amperian loop does not affect the value of the line integral, provided the enclosed current remains unchanged.

concept_notes.heading: Sign Convention for Enclosed Current
bullets: The direction of integration along the Amperian loop defines a positive sense via the right-hand screw rule.
Currents piercing the surface in the direction of the right-hand thumb curl are taken as positive.
Currents piercing in the opposite direction are taken as negative when computing the net enclosed current.

concept_notes.heading: Differential Form of Ampere's Law
bullets: Using Stokes' theorem, the line integral of B over a closed loop can be converted into a surface integral of the curl of B.
This yields ∇ × B = μ<sub>0</sub> J, where J is the free current density vector.
The differential form relates the local properties of the magnetic field directly to the local current density at any point.

derivations.title: Magnetic Field of an Infinite Long Straight Conductor
derivations.conditions: Steady current I flowing through an infinitely long, thin straight wire, evaluated at a radial distance r.
steps: By symmetry, the magnetic field lines are concentric circles centered on the wire, with B having a constant magnitude at a fixed radius r and pointing tangentially.
Choose a circular Amperian loop of radius r centered on the wire, coaxial with the conductor.
Evaluate the line integral: ∮ B · dl = ∮ B dl cos(0°) = B ∮ dl = B (2πr).
Equate this to μ<sub>0</sub> I<sub>enclosed</sub> according to Ampere's law, giving B (2πr) = μ<sub>0</sub> I.

derivations.title: Magnetic Field inside and outside a Long Solenoid
derivations.conditions: Solenoid of n turns per unit length carrying current I, assuming an infinitely long solenoid for edge-effect neglect.
steps: Argue that the magnetic field outside an ideal infinite solenoid is zero, and inside it is uniform and parallel to the axis.
Choose a rectangular Amperian loop of length l, with one side parallel to the axis inside the solenoid, the opposite side outside, and two sides perpendicular to the axis.
Evaluate the line integral along the four segments: only the segment inside the solenoid contributes to the integral, yielding B × l.
The total current enclosed by this rectangular loop is the number of turns inside length l multiplied by current I, which is (nl)I.

graphs_and_experiments.title: B versus r for a Long Straight Conductor
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph with radial distance r on the x-axis and magnetic field B on the y-axis. Inside the wire (r < R), B increases linearly with r. Outside the wire (r > R), B decreases hyperbolically as 1/r.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows the transition of magnetic field behavior from inside a solid current-carrying conductor to the external space.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in multiple choice questions regarding matching graphs to conductor geometries.

graphs_and_experiments.title: B versus r for a Toroidal Coil
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot showing zero magnetic field for r less than the inner radius, a 1/r decay profile within the core region, and zero field again for r greater than the outer radius.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the containment of the magnetic field entirely within the toroidal core.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to test understanding of boundary conditions and zero flux leakage in closed magnetic circuits.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Rowland Ring Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic or conceptual graph illustrating the measurement of magnetic induction B inside a toroidal specimen as a function of magnetizing field H.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Validates Ampere's circuital law applied to magnetic materials and helps determine relative permeability.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Theoretical questions on experimental setup for measuring magnetic properties of materials.

solved_numericals.question: A long straight wire carries a current of 10 A. Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic field at a distance of 5 cm from the wire.
solution_steps: Identify given values: I = 10 A, r = 5 cm = 0.05 m, μ<sub>0</sub> = 4π × 10<sup>-7</sup> T·m/A.
Apply the formula for a straight wire: B = (μ<sub>0</sub> I) / (2πr).

solved_numericals.question: A solenoid 50 cm long has 4 layers of windings of 400 turns each and carries a current of 2 A. Find the magnetic field at the center of the solenoid.
solution_steps: Calculate turns per unit length n: n = N / L = 1600 / 0.5 m = 3200 turns/m.
Use the solenoid formula: B = μ<sub>0</sub> n I.

solved_numericals.question: A long solid cylindrical wire of radius R = 2 cm carries a total current I = 5 A distributed uniformly across its cross-section. Calculate the magnetic field at a point r = 1 cm from the axis inside the wire.
solution_steps: Since the current is uniformly distributed, the current enclosed within radius r (1 cm) is proportional to the area ratio: I<sub>enclosed</sub> = I × (r<sup>2</sup> / R<sup>2</sup>).
Apply Ampere's law for inside a cylinder: B × (2πr) = μ<sub>0</sub> I<sub>enclosed</sub>.
Calculate final numerical value: B = (2 × 10<sup>-7</sup> × 1.25) / 0.01 = 2.5 × 10<sup>-5</sup> T.

assumptions_and_limitations: Ampere's circuital law in its standard form assumes steady-state currents (magnetostatics) where charge does not accumulate over time.
It fails when applied to circuits with changing electric fields unless the Maxwell displacement current term is included.
While the law holds true for any arbitrary closed loop, it is only analytically useful for highly symmetric current configurations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The magnetic field B in Ampere's law is produced only by the current enclosed by the Amperian loop.
common_misconceptions.correct: The magnetic field B at any point is the resultant field produced by ALL currents in the system, whereas the line integral of B depends solely on the enclosed current.
common_misconceptions.why: The line integral isolates the enclosed current due to vector cancellation properties, but the field vector itself obeys superposition from all sources.

common_misconceptions.wrong: If the net current enclosed by an Amperian loop is zero, the magnetic field B must be zero everywhere along the loop.
common_misconceptions.correct: A zero net enclosed current only guarantees that the line integral of B is zero, not that the magnetic field is zero at every point on the path.
common_misconceptions.why: Individual segments of the path can experience non-zero magnetic fields that cancel out algebraically over the complete closed loop.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Ampere's law can only be applied to circular loops.
common_misconceptions.correct: An Amperian loop can be of any arbitrary geometric shape, though symmetric shapes are chosen for ease of calculation.
common_misconceptions.why: The validity of the vector line integral theorem is independent of the contour shape, provided the surface bounded by it is continuous.

quick_revision: Ampere's law equates ∮ B · dl to μ<sub>0</sub> I<sub>enclosed</sub>.
For a long straight wire, B = μ<sub>0</sub>I / 2πr.
Inside an ideal infinite solenoid, B = μ<sub>0</sub>nI.
Addition of displacement current (ε<sub>0</sub> dΦ<sub>E</sub>/dt) completes Ampere's law for time-varying fields.
